reason: The narrative actually demonstrates the opposite moral framework. The Egyptian leader (Pharaoh) is portrayed as issuing unjust commands—enslaving the Hebrew people and ordering infanticide. The regular people—specifically the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah—are depicted as morally righteous for fearing God (וַתִּירֶ֤אןָ הַֽמְיַלְּדֹת֙ אֶת־ הָ֣אֱלֹהִ֔ים) and refusing to obey the Pharaoh's wicked decree. The text explicitly states they 'did not do as the king commanded' (וְלֹ֣א עָשׂ֔וּ כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר דִּבֶּ֥ר אֲלֵיהֶ֖ן מֶ֣לֶךְ מִצְרָ֑יִם) and God blessed them for this disobedience. The Hebrew mother similarly acts morally by protecting her son. The narrative validates the courage of ordinary people who resist unjust leadership, not the leaders who issue cruel commands.
